The paper develops a polemical and combative critique of psychoanalysis, as theory and as therapy, in terms of the ideas of modernity and postmodernity. The author paints a vivid theoretical fresco of the political deadlocks of our contemporary confessional culture, pitting psychoanalytic against constructivist approaches. An assessment of the dialogue between psychoanalysis and postmodernism is then offered. The author concludes by situating the radical political edge of psychoanalysis in terms of its insights into ethics, cultural difference and the project of human autonomy.

In order to motivate contemporary university students to consider possible avenues for social change, I have found that it is necessary to address openly student resistances to critical thinking and social consciousness. However, I have also discovered that any direct confrontation with the students' defense mechanisms can undermine the teacher-student relationship, and thus it is important to develop indirect methods for motivating students to overcome their resistances. In this essay, I will discuss how I have used computers and a psychoanalytic version of cultural studies to help students consider their roles in transforming various social inequities.

Eyal Rozmarin  

Manifesto for Philosophy, published in France in 1989 and in Norman Madarsz's translation to English in 1999, begins with a question: Is philosophy dead? The question is relevant because the claim that philosophy is dead is made often, by many philosophers. Badiou cites Lyotard's article titled “Philosophy as architecture is ruined.” He points out that Deleuze's last great book is about cinema and quotes Lacoue-Labarthe saying “One must no longer be in desire of philosophy” (p 28). The reasons for the all-but-complete turning away from philosophy are several. Philosophy is bankrupt because (since Nietzsche) God and the idea of the One that it stands for is dead, the category of the subject has been deconstructed, and the concept of truth has been disqualified from determining any reasonable discourse. Perhaps underlying it all, according to Badiou, philosophy is burdened to the point of extinction by the trauma of encountering the historic through Heidegger's thought, his National-Socialist involvement, and the un-explainable horrors of WWII. Faced with the task of explaining the world after the Holocaust and the role that philosophy may have played in generating ideas that made it possible, the philosophers determined that they could not do the job. But why philosophers, asks Badiou? “Neither scientists, a god many times in the dock, nor the military, nor even politicians have considered that the massacres of the century affected them as a body.” For some reason, “… our philosophers, taking on the burden of the century… have decided to plead guilty” (p 28).

Badiou does not offer a historical explanation for why this is the case. From a philosophical perspective, he suggests that the problem is in the idea that “everything is the concern of philosophy” (p 29). It is not, Badiou argues. Philosophy is not supposed to explain Auschwitz. This is the role of “an other order of thought,” (for example, the order of historicity) (p 30). At bottom, philosophy is facing a dilemma: operating under a megalomanic definition that necessarily results in its annihilation, or adopting a more modest definition that enables it to resume its project. Badiou's choice is clear - a return to a possible philosophy.

As Editors we are proud to present to you the launch issue of Psychoanalysis, Culture & Society (PCS), formerly called The Journal for the Psychoanalysis of Culture and Society (JPCS). With this issue, we celebrate a number of things: our move to Palgrave Macmillan Journals, our new editorial and international advisory boards of renowned academics and clinicians from around the world, and our new format. To create and celebrate this launch issue, we decided to ask members of our boards, including the board of the Association for the Psychoanalysis of Culture & Society (APCS), to write about their views on the relation between the psychic and the social worlds. As you will see, several of the essays are position papers, some of which are quite personal. As a group, they more than fulfill the mission of the journal, which is to embrace all schools of psychoanalysis and to focus our efforts on the way in which psychoanalysis can help us not only to understand the cultural problems that beset us but also to effect positive social change.

In keeping with our wish to publish clinical as well as academic psychoanalytic papers, this issue contains Elisabeth Young-Bruehl's (chair of the board of APCS and member of the international advisory board of the journal) conceptualization of the variety of forms of child maltreatment and how they intertwine. Her case example shows the limitations of the usual nosological categories of child abuse. Kareen Ror Malone (an associate editor of PCS) and Shannon D. Kelly critique, from a Lacanian perspective, a recently published relational clinical paper on the psychic effects of changes in family structure. Their larger purpose is to caution against the importation into clinical work of ideological frameworks, even when those frameworks are “alternative.” Also bridging the clinical and the academic worlds is the paper by Lynne Layton (editor of PCS)

This article examines the possibility of political change through the examination of ontological concepts pertaining to the social as drawn from the thought of Lacan and Deleuze. Distinguishing between the virtual and the actual, I argue that a politics of the actual, which is premised on conflicts between social groups, fails to produce real social change by leaving the virtual social structure organizing relationships between these groups intact. By contrast, a politics of the virtual makes these structures the direct object of its struggle, and seeks to determine the void underlying social relations as the place where real change is possible.

On Sacredness and Transgression: Understanding Social Antagonism

Margarita Palacios

Margarita Palacios

Vergara 210, Santiago, Chile
E-mail: mpalaciosb@yahoo.com

Margarita Palacios   Chair of the Sociology Department at the University Diego Portales in Santiago de Chile. She holds a Ph.D. in Sociology from New School University. Her research focuses on the relation between collective violence and enjoyment.
social theory; law; violence; social antagonism; identity; fantasy

In this paper, I argue that in order to theorize violence it is necessary to consider not only the “contingent/historical” character of particular expressions of violence, but also the more “permanent/meta-historical” character of social identities. That is, it is necessary not only to look at identities already constituted, but at the very process of constitution of social identities itself. Only then it is possible to see the schism that is inherent to every social identity. This schism between the particular (the empirical) and the universal (the transcendental moral horizon, which allows the articulation of social life) is what accounts for both freedom/social change and social antagonism. Social antagonism, expressed as social exclusion and violence, is a reaction to the fear of “social disintegration”; that is, the fear of the possibility of losing the “universal/moral horizon” that makes society possible. Further, I argue that violence expresses a paradoxical dynamic between morality and enjoyment. At the same time that it attempts to restore the threatened symbolic order (that makes society possible), violence constitutes the ultimate transgression of that symbolic order.

For others, creative writing courses help students understand literary devices with better clarity and interest. Still others link the creative functions of all types of written expression together; the act of expression becomes the focus of what is creative.

To creative writing teachers, psychoanalysis represents many things as well.

It is my pleasure to review Muriel Dimen's new book, Sexuality, Intimacy, Power, published by The Analytic Press in 2003. An ambitious, sweeping effort by an author whose scholarly reputation in the field of gender studies and postmodern psychoanalysis is undisputed, the book is also candid and charming, with Dimen vividly illustrating aspects of dense theory with poignant vignettes from her work with patients as well as from her own rich and colorful personal history. As Dimen points out, her own life has been marked by the upheaval of socio-cultural events of the countercultural late 60's, and she shares with us her insights into how her life serves to illustrate one of her main themes: that “the personal is political is theoretical” (p 201).

In organizing her book, Dimen stresses that her topics of sexuality, intimacy and power will be addressed from three perspectives: psychoanalysis, feminism and social theory. Throughout, a multidisciplinary perspective (Dimen is an anthropologist as well as a psychoanalyst) informs the author's discourse as she offers glimpses of her personal and intellectual journey in feminist-Marxism-socialism, illustrating how these experiences have shaped her understanding of her thesis. Her politically conscious perspective is declared in her preface, “Personal Journey From Duality to Multiplicity.” Dimen deconstructs the binary, noting that it always conceals a hierarchy. She further asserts that duality is a “set-up” because it leads us to “want to know which pole is true” (p 7). Dimen believes that it is more useful to replace either/or with both/and - in the interest of creating a transitional space in which all aspects of a potential idea can be explored.

As one examines the various sections of the volume, one is reminded of Derrida's famous epigram, “There is too much truth”; it is clear that Dimen is striving to create a new experience for the reader as she moves from deconstruction of familiar postmodern themes towards a fresh construction with an enlivening coherence, resulting in a collage of narrative multiplicity. One of the characteristics that differentiates and, I think, distinguishes Dimen from other American postmodern feminist psychoanalytic thinkers is her relative emphasis on aspects of power and class - particularly, the political - that shape our experience of gender and sexuality, and, in turn, influence our experience of intimacy. Here she brings her training as a cultural anthropologist to bear as she emphasizes the many ways in which an individual's immersion in one's socio-cultural milieu may shape one's individual psychology and psychopathology. That is, unlike many psychoanalytic writers, Dimen is particularly mindful of how culture shapes the individual: from Freud into the present, the more typical perspective of the psychoanalyst, especially when in the consulting room, has been to examine the influence of the individual on cultural development and expression.

In this paper, we focus on the ways in which subjective investments in whiteness work to construct Indigenous people as threats to the white Australian nation. In order to better understand such subjective investments, we employ an approach to analysing talk that draws upon both psychoanalysis and discursive psychology. We suggest that this combination may allow for a thoroughly social understanding of the practices of exclusion within Australia. Slavoj Žižek's critical examination of today's liberal-democratic capitalist ideology highlights the phenomenon of “cynical distance,” namely, a position where the individual consciously professes disbelief in relation to the status quo system while nonetheless behaving “as if” he/she really accepts the authority of this system. Unconsciously, such cynical subjects, Žižek maintains, are fervent believers in the ideologies that they overtly claim to disregard. Drawing on Marx, Freud, and Lacan, Žižek scrutinizes the structural relations between cynicism, disavowal, and belief in order to show how commodity fetishism and the attribution of one's unconscious beliefs to others enable one to ultimately accept acquiescence to the reigning state of the situation. However, in both decoupling Marx's descriptive-diagnostic discourse on capitalism from his positive prescriptive program as well as basing his own political thought on the Lacanian notion of the Act, Žižek's thought is itself in danger of falling into the trap of cynical distance.

Lacan's Concept of the Real of Jouissance: Clinical Illustrations and Implications

Frédéric Declercq

Frédéric Declercq

H. Dunantlaan, 2, 9000 Ghent, Belgium E-mail: frederic.declercq@UGent.be

Frédéric Declercq   Assistant Professor at the Department of Psychoanalysis and Clinical consulting at the University of Ghent. He teaches courses on Psychodiagnostics, Sexuality and sexual disturbances and Models in Psychoanalysis from a Freudian Lacanian point of View. His research interests are Lacan's return to Freud as well as Post Traumatic Stress Disorders from a Freudian-Lacanian framework. He is a forensic expert at the Court of First Instance and the magistrate's court. Psychopathy is also one of his research areas. He is a psychoanalyst in private practice.
jouissance, body, aetiology, traversal, primary phantasy, suppression

In his return to Freud, the early Lacan focussed on the symbolic and the imaginary. Reflecting mainly on the symbolic structure of the unconscious, the conversion symptoms and the (phallic) jouissance, his references to their real dimension are few and far between. From seminar XI (1964) onwards, though, the real - and more specifically the real of the drives - is given more attention. It is at this point, when elaborating the real dimension of jouissance, that the concept of the real of the body intervenes. With the real of the body, the accent lies on the cut and alienated relation between the subject and jouissance. At first, this polarisation of the subject and its body serves Lacan's aim of situating the exact place of jouissance. Amongst other things this will enable him to determine the role played by culture and society in the genesis of neuroses. Further, the concept of the real of body has to do with the crucial question of aetiology, since the real of the drives is the cornerstone of psychopathological symptoms. As such, Lacan's notion of the real of the body picks up again and develops the crucial concept of fixation, which Freud left unfinished.

The problem of the psychic and the social is the problem of the third, and the third is a problem of dualism. This point is illustrated with regard to both clinic and theory. Among her books are Anna Freud: A Biography; Creative Characters; The Anatomy of Prejudices; Cherishment (with Faith Bethelard); and the recently published (2003) Where Do We Fall When We Fall in Love?
child abuse and neglect; child sexual abuse; psychoanalytic treatment; nosology of child maltreatment; prejudice

This case of an adult who as a child suffered maltreatment within three basically different types of relationships is offered as an opening to reconsider psychoanalytically the forms of maltreatment that have become standard over the last four decades in the field of “Child Abuse and Neglect” (CAN), that is, physical abuse, neglect, sexual abuse, and emotional abuse. It is suggested that the patient experienced her maltreaters as intending to eliminate her, to force her to play adult roles, and to erase her identity for narcissistic purposes. A nosology keyed to these types of intentions and relations, it is hypothesized, might make a better guide to clinical work with abuse victims generally than the standard classification of abuse and neglect types, and would also allow such clinical work to connect with social theory of prejudices.

Bion, Habermas, political action, projective identification, genetic engineering

Politics suggests a common purpose that binds individuals into a group with a collective conviction, based on principle. Psychoanalysis is concerned with the character of the internal world and with how society sees itself: common purpose may be an idealization and conviction may rest on narcissism, supported by projection. Habermas has explored the right of parents genetically to design their children (a conviction), and the implications for the children's identity and, especially, for the “ethical self-understanding of the species” that allows it (a social self-reflection). This paper develops Habermas' theme in the direction of a psychoanalytic self-awareness in society. It compares the sense of common purpose and conviction with a pluralism, arguing that the former is supported by “projective communication”, while the latter is conflicted in its sense of purpose and conviction, and is supported by “informative communication”. Projective communication undermines the tolerant political process of informative communication, and psychoanalytic self-awareness mitigates these destructive tendencies.

Paul LePhuoc  

Considering its role in the consolidation of the Western heterosexual male psyche and the concomitant abjection of difference through misogynistic, heteronormative, and racist discourses - what might psychoanalysis have to offer the political efforts of feminist, queer and postcolonial theory? Jan Campbell approaches these questions through a carefully researched engagement with some of the most pivotal theoretical debates and impasses within psychoanalysis and their corresponding tensions with political and cultural theory. She weaves together otherwise isolated strands of psychoanalytic theory that have become rigidly dichotomized along theoretical “party lines,” and challenges the premises of these polarizations - arguing that they have compromised the political possibilities for psychoanalytic theory. Over eight densely packed chapters, she constructs a series of innovative bridges between a staggeringly broad spectrum of theorists and their interlocutors across queer, feminist, and post-colonial theory, resulting in a deeply suggestive reworking of psychoanalytic theory.

Cast as ahistorical, apolitical, quietist, and defeatist, psychoanalysis has often been rejected by those seeking political and social change. From the originary tensions between Freud and Marx, political theory and theories of the unconscious have often been regarded as incommensurable. Nonetheless, increasing recognition of the dynamism of the subject and its non-correspondence with discursive and practical orders has highlighted the inadequacy of social and materialist analyses that neglect to theorize the complexities of subjectivity and the unconscious. Campbell executes a balanced and sophisticated negotiation of these well-worn tensions. She writes: “If Lacanian psychoanalysis can be faulted for refusing the historical experience of the body, then a more socialist analysis may also be censured for situating that body so passively and refusing the unconscious a dynamic role” (28). Campbell labors to historicize psychoanalysis and its theories of the unconscious by focusing on the ascendancy of Lacanian theory - across feminist, queer and postcolonial theory - and exposing its overwhelming dependence on (and she argues, reactivity toward and reification of) the repressive and negative dimensions of the Oedipal complex and phallic dominance.

Deborah Anna Luepnitz explicitly sets out to describe the elasticity of human nature, the complex movement between connection and isolation. Luepnitz achieves this goal and imbeds within it another task that makes this book important and compelling reading. In addition to a detailed examination of intimacy and its vicissitudes, this book offers a microscopic observation of cultural process as manifest within the individual. Intimacy's dilemmas are shown to have sociocultural antecedents.

Luepnitz organizes her book around the central metaphor of the porcupine, borrowed from Schopenhauer who used it to delineate the problem with human intimacy. According to Schopenhauer, people are like porcupines that rush together to shield themselves from the cold, only to pierce each other with their quills. The pain they inflict upon each other as they huddle together causes them to break away from the shelter and security of each other's warmth. Luepnitz provides five clinical vignettes to describe the human process of coming together and breaking apart, and the pain caused therein. While the porcupine metaphor strikingly organizes the ideas and language of this book, what is equally exciting is how Luepnitz demonstrates cultural process resonating in the psyche of an individual or couple. The other aspect to Schopenhauer's porcupine metaphor is the role of will, the ability of humans to act on desire rather than reason alone.

Schopenhauer's conception of human will suggests that we are somewhat doomed by our natural tendency to behave like the lesser-evolved porcupines. People, according to Schopenhauer, will continually and repetitively seek sanctuary from the porcupines that quill us.

A debate between Lynne Segal and Juliet Mitchell is the starting point of this inquiry into different notions about the nature of the unconscious. The paper argues that unconscious conflict derives both from universal sources and from historical contingencies, but that it is largely the latter that is the origin of neurotic misery (as opposed to “common” human unhappiness). Using clinical examples, the paper elaborates a relational perspective on unconscious processes and analytic treatment, at the center of which is the repetition compulsion. After discussing different theories about the relation between the psychic and the social, the paper proposes that the concept of normative unconscious processes provides a useful way to think about the link between social norms and subjective psychic reality.

This paper explores psychoanalytic renditions of the concept of envy as an emotion. The term envy is used to mean many different things in everyday language but in psychoanalysis its meaning is far more specific - envy is an expression, projection and deflection of Thanatos - the death drive. This is a particularly important concept in Kleinian psychoanalysis as envy blocks the very possibility of love existing at all by destroying all that is good. This can have serious social consequences and the second half of this paper addresses envy in racism, politics and everyday life relating the concept to the social arena and social action.

Psychoanalysis can be considered from three different viewpoints: first as a science and a theory of psychic functioning, secondly as an ethical system, and thirdly as a clinical practice. In this paper, we argue that these three perspectives are deeply inter-related, since they have everything to do with a fundamental structural underlying lack. We discuss why and how psychoanalytic ethics need to assume this lack, how the original contribution psychoanalysis can make to science is related to the study of it, and how psychoanalytic practice is faced with the continuous challenge of starting from the lack as a source of creativity.
